---
title: "Trait-gradient analysis"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5)
```

The trait-gradient analysis of Ackerly & Cornwell (2007) places each species along the
gradient defined by the mean trait of the communities it lives in. The species mean
\(\bar t_i\) splits into \(\beta_i\), the mean of the communities of the species, and
\(\alpha_i = \bar t_i - \beta_i\), its difference from the species it co-occurs with. The
gradient is built from the trait itself, so no environmental variable has to be chosen
beforehand. \(\beta\) measures where a species sorts among communities, and \(\alpha\)
measures how it differs within them.

`trait_gradient()` follows the original analysis with three changes, described in its help
page: site means leave out the focal species, the weights of site means and of species means
are chosen apart, and the tests use a null model with fixed margins and a phylogenetic model
that carries the sampling error of each value. The results below are simulated.

```{r}
library(comdynamite)

set.seed(1)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(30)
sim <- simulate_metacommunity(landscape_implicit(25), species_traits(tree, lambda = 1),
                              competition_matrix(tree, "none"), n_steps = 100,
                              seed_steps = 1:5)
ind <- sample_individuals(sim, n = 5, local_adaptation = 0.5, intraspecific_sd = 1)
tg <- trait_gradient(ind, abundance = "abundance")
tg
```

## The gradient

Each grey point is a population, at the mean of its site without the species itself. Lines
are the slopes of species over the range of their sites, and large points are the species
means at \((\beta_i, \bar t_i)\). Species above the dashed line have positive \(\alpha\):
they carry larger values than the species they live with.

```{r}
plot(tg)
```

## Leaving the focal species out

With the focal species inside the site means, \(\beta_i\) contains \(\bar t_i\). In poor sites
this ties \(\beta\) to the trait of the species and makes \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\) look more
related than they are.

```{r}
original <- trait_gradient(ind, abundance = "abundance", leave_one_out = FALSE)
c(leave_one_out = cor(tg$species$beta, tg$species$alpha),
  original = cor(original$species$beta, original$species$alpha))
```

## Weights

Abundance weights let the dominant species set the gradient. `trait_gradient_weights()` runs
the four combinations of weights for sites and species and correlates them with the first.

```{r}
trait_gradient_weights(ind, abundance = "abundance")$correlation
```

## Null model

`trait_gradient_test()` moves species among sites with the curveball algorithm, which keeps
the richness of every site and the number of sites of every species. Populations keep their
trait values and abundances when they move.

```{r}
test <- trait_gradient_test(tg, n_null = 199)
test
plot(test)
```

## Phylogeny

`trait_gradient_phylo()` asks whether \(\beta\), \(\alpha\) and the species mean are
conserved. Each value has a bootstrap standard error, added to the covariance of the model,
so a species seen in few sites does not pass for fast evolution.

```{r}
ph <- trait_gradient_phylo(tg, tree, n_boot = 199)
ph
```

In this simulation the optima evolve by Brownian motion (`lambda = 1`), so \(\beta\), which
follows the optima, should prefer Brownian motion over the model without phylogeny.

## References

Ackerly, D. D., & Cornwell, W. K. (2007). A trait-based approach to community assembly:
partitioning of species trait values into within- and among-community components.
*Ecology Letters*, 10, 135–145. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2006.01006.x

Strona, G., Nappo, D., Boccacci, F., Fattorini, S., & San-Miguel-Ayanz, J. (2014). A fast and
unbiased procedure to randomize ecological binary matrices with fixed row and column totals.
*Nature Communications*, 5, 4114. https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms5114
